title: Midlife Exercise and Blood Sugar Control Linked to Slower Cognitive Decline, Study Finds
excerpt: A long-term study from UT Health San Antonio found that physical activity and maintaining healthy fasting glucose levels in middle age are associated with significantly slower rates of cognitive decline later in life, with notable differences across ethnic groups.
body:
• Any level of physical activity in midlife is associated with slower cognitive decline in later years, with especially strong effects among Hispanic adults.
  • Maintaining fasting blood glucose at or below 126 mg/dL in midlife is linked to slower cognitive decline among non-Hispanic white adults.
  • Nearly 40% of Alzheimer's cases may be attributable to modifiable risk factors, with cardiovascular health playing a central role in brain aging.
  • Hispanic older adults remain underrepresented in Alzheimer's research despite facing a disproportionate burden of the disease.

Physical activity and blood sugar management during middle age may play a significant role in protecting cognitive function decades later, according to new research from UT Health San Antonio published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: Behavior & Socioeconomics of Aging.

The study, which followed 402 San Antonio residents with a mean age of 57.9 years, found that both exercise and glucose control were associated with slower rates of cognitive decline — but the strongest patterns differed by ethnicity, highlighting the importance of population-specific prevention strategies.

Key Findings Across Ethnic Groups

Among the study's participants, 52% were Hispanic and the remainder non-Hispanic white. Approximately 58.5% were women. Researchers found that any physical activity — including simply avoiding a sedentary lifestyle — was particularly associated with slower cognitive decline among Mexican American participants.

For non-Hispanic white participants, the key factor was fasting blood glucose. Readings at or below 126 milligrams per deciliter were linked to a measurably slower rate of cognitive decline.

"Our findings suggest that engaging in any level of physical activity and potentially maintaining optimal fasting blood glucose levels in midlife are associated with a significantly slower rate of cognitive decline in late life."

— Janette Vazquez, Ph.D., Glenn Biggs Institute for Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases

Addressing the Alzheimer's Burden

The study arrives at a critical juncture. Alzheimer's disease currently affects 6.7 million people in the United States, and rising life expectancy combined with an aging population is driving prevalence upward. Recent estimates attribute nearly 40% of Alzheimer's cases to modifiable risk factors, with cardiovascular health emerging as a major influence on brain aging.

The American Heart Association's Life's Simple 7 framework — encompassing diet, smoking status, physical activity, blood pressure, BMI, cholesterol, and fasting glucose — served as the study's measurement tool. Previous research has linked higher scores on this framework with better cognitive performance and reduced dementia risk, though those associations have not been uniform across populations.

Hispanic Communities Bear Disproportionate Risk

The research underscores a significant health disparity. About 14% of Hispanic adults aged 65 and older have Alzheimer's disease, compared with 10% of non-Hispanic white adults in the same age group. Mexican Americans, the largest Hispanic population in the United States, also carry elevated rates of diabetes, obesity, and dyslipidemia — all conditions that increase dementia risk.

Despite these disparities, Hispanic communities remain underrepresented in Alzheimer's research, limiting the development of targeted prevention strategies.

"By improving cardiovascular health through modifiable lifestyle changes, there is a potential to meaningfully alleviate the public health burden of Alzheimer's disease and other dementias, particularly in high-risk populations."

— Claudia Satizabal, Ph.D., UT Health San Antonio

Decades of Data from South Texas

The study drew on participants from two landmark UT Health San Antonio projects: the San Antonio Heart Study, which tracked more than 5,000 people from 1979 through the 2000s to investigate type 2 diabetes and heart disease, and the San Antonio Longitudinal Study of Aging, which followed older participants from that earlier cohort.

Researchers assessed cognitive function up to four times using the Mini-Mental State Examination, an 11-question screening tool that evaluates memory, attention, and thinking skills. Their statistical models accounted for age, sex, income, and education, with additional sensitivity analyses to check whether participants leaving the study early could have skewed results.

What Comes Next

Because the associations between cardiovascular factors and cognitive decline differed by ethnicity, the researchers say larger, more diverse studies are needed to replicate the findings. Vazquez noted that tracking cardiovascular health across an entire lifespan, rather than at a single point in time, could yield deeper insights into how cognitive decline develops differently across populations.

The study was supported by the T32 training grant in Pathobiology of Occlusive Vascular Disease, the San Antonio Heart and Mind Study, the San Antonio Longitudinal Study of Aging, and the Burroughs Wellcome Fund Postdoctoral Diversity Enrichment Program.
